Over 3 hours of video, plus cheatsheets and tips and tricks for success with your machine.

At first glance, any knitting machine seems complicated. Think about the dashboard in a car. There are lots of dials and buttons and levers, but once you learn the names of things you'll quickly discover what you need to make the car go.

Before you start to set up your machine, identify the tools and accessories that came with your machine.
If you don't have the tools marked "essential" you'll be able to get started knitting, but ask Mr. Google to help you find them.
When looking for tools and fun accessories, keep in mind that this is a Brother/Knit King 4.5mm gauge machine.
Essential:
  • Table Clamps
  • Needle Pusher
  • Latch Tool
  • Transfer Tools
  • Claw weights
  • Oil (sewing machine oil works great)
  • Power Cord
Consider Locating:
  • Carriage lock - good for securing the carriage when packing it
  • Ravel Cord - "must have" for certain techniques (use any smooth, strong cord - ie Bedspread Crochet cotton)
  • Wax - Helps reduce static and makes knitting some yarns easier
  • Extra needles - Nice to have on hand - you won't break needles often, but ...
  • Latch Opening Plate (used with the ribber)
  • Cast on Comb
  • Plaiting yarn Feeder

The 4.5 mm gauge of this machine (standard gauge) uses lighter weight yarns. Consider lace weight or sock weight yarn. In some parts of the world a yarn for this machine is named 4-Ply.

You can choose a lighter weight yarn and knit it at a very loose tension for a lightweight fabric. You can knit the same yarn at a tighter tension for a very different look. The fiber, color and texture of the yarn is up to you.

The only limit is the size of the needles. If the yarn is too thick and doesn't fit in the hooks of the needles, it can split and/or jam the machine.

Take a moment to get familiar with the terminology and location of items on the carriage

Don't be overwhelmed by all the buttons, dials and levers on the carriage. As we cover the various techniques available, we will walk through each setting and explore it's impact on your knitting.
Instead of forming each stitch one-at-a-time like in hand knitting, the carriage acts as your hands and fingers.
  • Using the butts of the needle and the channels underneath the carriage, select which needles will knit.

  • The Tension dial controls how the yarn is fed and how large the stitches will be.

  • The Change Knob Tells the machine that you want to knit in pattern

  • The Cam buttons instruct the machine about what type of stitch pattern you want to create
As you continue on your journey to master your machine, all of the other settings will become second nature to you.

Change Knob (KC knob) In general this Knob instructs the machine to "read" the stitch pattern and select needles for patterning
  • N-L: Normal (plain) and lace
  • KC (I): Selects the end needles according to the pattern
  • KC (II) Prevents the end needles from patterning
  • CR: (Carriage Release) allows you to lift and remove the carriage from the machine
legacyFields.SPOT_TEXT_6:
Cam Button Release Lever
When engaged, the Cam buttons (Tuck, part, Mc/L) are pushed in. To quickly release them use the release lever. It's marked "plain" as a reminder that to knit plain (stockinette) you don't want the cam buttons engaged.
legacyFields.SPOT_TEXT_7:
Holding Cam Lever
With this lever engaged, needles in "D" position will not knit. Used for partial knitting and intarsia.
legacyFields.SPOT_TEXT_8:
Cam Buttons
Hand -in-hand with the Change Knob (which selects needles), the cam buttons determine how stitches are formed based on the needle positions.
For example, when the Tuck buttons are engaged, selected needles do not knit and the yarn passes OVER the needles (tucking). When the Part buttons are engaged, selected needles do not knit and the working yarn passes UNDER the needles (slipping)

Used for "picture knitting" allowing you to knit multiple colors across the row without floats.

components.html:
Understanding how to set your carriage for PLAIN KNITTING is essential
It is a good habit to always check your carriage settings before starting a new technique or a new piece of knitting. It's easy to have your carriage set for patterning, then come back days later and be surprised that the machine isn't knitting as expected.
Take time every time you sit down to knit and double check the settings.

Save your back, neck and shoulders
In the videos in this course, you'll see me pushing the carriage with one hand. BAD!!!! I'm reaching around the camera.
When you are knitting use both hands and push and pull alternately to move the carriage.
Many knitters also adjust their knitting table so they can stand while knitting.

Arm, hand and wrist position

STOP! LOOK AT THE POSITION OF YOUR HAND AND WRIST IN RELATION TO YOUR ELBOW.Many knitters will find their elbow is below the level of the wrist and hand.
Knitting in this position, after a time, will create an ache and pain through the neck and across the shoulders. Try sitting higher so that your elbow is slightly above the wrist and hand.

More tips

  • A stool for your feet may be needed or your machine table or stand may have to be lowered.

  • If you have a stand to use your machine, the same elbow position is needed. (elbows slightly above the hands)

  • Try standing to knit. Use an adjustable table to keep the elbow position correct. Here's what I use

  • Good lighting is a must

  • A clean (and oiled) machine bed and carriage are essential.

The sponge bar (needle retaining bar) holds the needles in place for proper stitch formation.
Anytime you start using a used machine, the first thing to check is the condition of the spongebar. Even if the machine hasn't been used much, the sponge can deteriorate.
Also check the condition of the needles - no rust and no bent or broken needles.

The Automatic Patterning Device (Electronics / Operation Panel)
is the brains behind automatic stitch patterning on your machine.
No mystery here. The digital instructions (on/off, black/white, 0:1) determine which needles are selected to be used for stitch patterning based on the carriage settings.

With Automatic patterning, the "brains" of the machine reads the stitch pattern and selects needles. The selected needles are then manipulated based on the Cam Button settings to create the following stitch types.
  • Stockinette Stitch
  • Tuck | Pull Up
  • Slip Stitch
  • Knit-In | Fairisle
  • Thread Lace | Punch Lace
  • Knit Weave | Lay-In
  • Plaiting
  • Intarsia | Picture Knitting

Two Ways to Use Stitch Patterns

1. Use Built-In Stitch Patterns

Depending on your machine’s memory, you may have up to 550 built-in stitch patterns. Each pattern has a number you can look up in the Stitch World 1 book.

Use the variation keys to change how an electronic stitch pattern knits. If you’re just getting started, practice with the built-in patterns first so you can see how they work.

2. Create Your Own Stitch Patterns

Once you’re comfortable knitting the built-in patterns, try designing your own. You can enter a design in two ways:

  • Enter it on the machine. Use the “beep-beep-beep” method to enter one repeat, stitch by stitch and row by row.
  • Use stitch design software. Create the pattern on your computer with DesignaKnit or Cochenille Stitch Designer, then download it to your machine.

Before you design your own patterns, learn how each stitch technique works and what your machine can do. That will help you create a pattern your machine can knit.

Open Cast On

An open cast on leaves stitches that can unravel. Some machine manuals include instructions for this type of cast on. The previous video shows an open cast on with a cast-on comb.

Here are three variations:

  • Open cast on with a cast-on comb (shown in the video)
  • Open cast on with a wire
  • Open cast on with ravel cord

Most knitters move beyond those methods pretty quickly. Here are two methods you’ll use again and again to leave stitches open for later:

  • Scrap and ravel
  • Using a cast-on rag

You can pick up the open stitches and hand knit ribbing. Or turn the knitting, pick up the open stitches, and knit reverse stockinette.

Closed Cast On

A closed cast on secures the starting stitches.

Closed but Temporary

These methods are handy for swatching or when the cast-on edge won’t be the finished edge of your project.

  • Cast on for swatching
  • Scrap ’n Ravel cast on
  • Cut ’n Sew

Closed and Functional

Use these methods when you want a finished edge that needs no additional finishing.

  • E-wrap cast on (many variations)
  • Chain cast on

No matter what cast on method you use, it's important to secure the yarn tail when casting on so the first few stitches knit correctly.
Use the arrows to navigate

components.html:
Swatching Is Essential

A swatch gives you a chance to test your yarn and settings before you start a project. Use swatches to:

  • Establish stitch and row gauge
  • Test stitch patterns
  • Practice techniques
  • Estimate how much yarn you’ll need

Knit a Practice Swatch

  1. Set your row counter to 000.
  2. Thread the mast with your working yarn. Check that the yarn flows smoothly through the mast.
  3. Thread the carriage using the A feeder.
  4. Cast on 60 stitches using your preferred cast-on method.
  5. Knit to RC:080.
  6. Bind off.

As you knit: Move the carriage at an even speed and avoid taking it too far past either edge of the knitting.

Make yourself a cheat sheet with the printable reference card (PDF)

When you are just getting started exploring your machine, the number of stitches to cast on and rows to knit isn't critical. Measuring over 40 stitches and 60 rows is the recommended standard for your machine. This standard was established by using a Gauge Ruler to measure gauge.
No matter how you measure, establishing gauge IS CRITICAL to success with your knitting machine.

To knit a "proper" swatch (in any stitch pattern)

  1. Cast on 60 stitches with the method of your choice
  2. Knit 10 rows with your garment yarn
  3. Knit 2 rows with a contrasting color (similar weight yarn)
  4. Knit 20 rows. Isolate and mark 40 stitches (needles L21 and R21)
  5. Knit 20 rows. Isolate and mark 40 stitches
  6. Knit 20 rows. (a total of 60 rows after the contrasting row)
  7. Knit 2 rows with a contrasting color
  8. Knit 10 rows with the garment yarn
  9. Bind off (this is a good time to practice different bind off methods)

Using a Gauge ruler makes quick work of measuring gauge.
Construct your own gauge ruler to measure swatches over 40 stitches and 60 rows.

All of these buttons will become second nature to you.
Just take it step-by-step.

Overview

To program your own stitch pattern, use the control panel to copy your design from a grid, one stitch and one row at a time.

  • The machine assigns pattern numbers 901 through 998 to custom stitch patterns.
  • A pattern can be 1 to 200 stitches wide, up to the number of needles on the machine.
  • Plan the number of rows before you start. Larger designs take longer to enter.
  • You can edit or delete custom stitch patterns.
  • Give the machine a moment to respond when working with a large pattern.
  • You’re entering a black-and-white motif, one square at a time. Keep your design sheet handy because the control panel doesn’t display the full motif.

Printable Design Sheets

Brother supplied a pad of design sheets with the machine. Use this graph paper to sketch and record your stitch patterns, then follow your sketch as you enter the pattern on the Brother 940.

We can knit so much more than plain stockinette with this machine. The digital, automatic patterning mechanism can automatically create textured and multi-color stitch patterns.
It is critical that you understand the 3 elements that create stitch patterns.
3 settings control stitch patterning:
1
Needle position
2
Change Knob
3
Cam Buttons

1
Needle position
Letters marked on the side of the needlebed A-B-D-E represent:
A Out of Work Position (Non-working Position |NWP) Unused Needles
B Working Position (WP) Needles lined up to knit in stockinette and most stitch patterns
D Middle Position(MP) (Pattern Position) Bring the needles from holding position into working and pattern work positions
E Holding Position (HP) The farthest position from "A" on the needlebed

Because this is a Brother machine, the needles are automatically pre-selected when working in pattern. On the previous row we can preview what needles will be involved in the stitch pattern. (Unlike Singer/Silver/Studio machines)

2
Change Knob
The Change Knob instructs the machine that you are going to be knitting in pattern. This setting COMBINED WITH the Cam Buttons create stitch patterning on your machine.
N-L Plain Knitting (stockinette) and Lace knitting
KC (I) (Knit Card I) for stitch patterns that use needle selection
End needles will always stay in "D"/Middle Position
KC(II) (Knit Card II) for stitch patterns that use needle selection
End needles will follow the stitch pattern
CR (carriage release) Release the carriage from the needlebed

About End Needle Selection

3
Cam Buttons
The Cam Buttons control the action of the needles for specific stitch types.
N / H N="normal"
H=Holds needles in "E" position (both directions)
Plain Releases (cancels) all Cam buttons
Tuck Positions needles for tuck both left and right or independently
MC (Top button only) used for Fairisle Patterns
L (both center buttons) used for knitting with the Lace Carriage
Part Positions needles for SLIP (skip) both left and right or independently

CR Key Temporarily stops the row count and allows the input of the number of rows to adjust Start and re-start stitch patterning after fixing mistakes
Arrows Increases and decreases the current stitch pattern row number Adjusts the stitch pattern row number any time needed.

Overview:

Programming your own stitch patterns is a matter of using the control panel to enter the data stitch-by-stitch and row-by-row.
You will be copying a grid using the buttons in the control panel.
  • The computer assigns stitch numbers 901 - 998 for custom stitches
  • The pattern can be from 1 to 200 stitches (the number of needles available)
  • The size of the stitch pattern is "unlimited" (or limited to your patience level)
  • Custom stitch patterns can be edited and deleted
  • This is 80's technology, be patient, there may be a delay in responding with large stitch patterns
  • Although you can't view it, you are "electronically" reproducing a black and white motif.
Supplied with the machines was a printed pad of "Design Sheets". These were graph paper to use for sketching out and recording stitch designs.
Follow the sketch when inputting your own custom stitch patterns in the 940 electronics.

Start by drawing/copying a stitch pattern on a Design Sheet.
Count the number of stitches and rows in the design (be aware of how repeats will align). Note any color changes
Check your stitch pattern BEFORE adding yarn by "dry knitting".

One you've chosen and positioned a stitch pattern in the machine's electronics, you need to communicate to the machine that you are ready to knit.
Just because you've chosen stitch pattern #100, the machine doesn't yet know what technique you are using (tuck, slip, fairisle, etc). The CAM BUTTONS control how the stitches are formed based on the needle selections made by the electronics.
3 settings control stitch patterning:
1
Needle position (stitch pattern)
2
Change Knob (KC)
3
Cam Buttons (slip, tuck, fairisle, etc)

The steps:
Establish and position the stitch pattern
Carriage on the left, Change Knob to KC(I) or KC(II)
"Memorize" the pattern (pass the carriage past the Turn Mark)
Knit to the right (needles should be selected)
Set Cam Buttons as needed
Continue knitting

Being able to knit and measure accurate swatches is ESSENTIAL to your success with your machine.
Make time to learn to swatch in pattern

Don't skip this!

Being able to move the carriage without knitting or dropping stitches is essential to fixing mistakes and shaping necklines.
Let's say you just ripped out a row (or a few) or you put some knitting back on the needlebed (from a garter bar or waste yarn) or for some other reason, the working yarn is on the opposite side from the carriage. Learn to safely position the carriage without taking it of the needlebed.

Try this yourself

Free pass in plain knitting
  • Knit a few inches in plain knitting
  • Rip out 1 row (working yarn opposite the carriage)
  • Free Pass

Free pass in Tuck or Slip
  • Establish a tuck or slip stitch pattern for a few inches
  • Rip out 2 rows
  • Free pass to position the carriage to the left
  • Use the CR key to re-establish the correct stitch pattern row number
  • Free pass to re-memorize and arrange the pattern needles
  • Continue Knitting with no interruption to the pattern design

Free pass in Fairisle
  • Establish a 2 color Fairisle stitch pattern for a few inches
  • Rip out 2 rows
  • Free pass to position the carriage to the left
  • Use the CR key to re-establish the correct stitch pattern row number
  • Free pass to re-memorize and arrange the pattern needles
  • Re-thread the carriage with both yarns
  • MC button in
  • Continue Knitting with no interruption to the pattern design

blocks.title: Stop and Start for Necklines: The Basics

components.html:
Overview

Use the Free Pass technique to pause stitch patterning while you shape one side of the neckline, then resume the pattern on the other side.

  1. Divide the knitting and scrap off the stitches as directed by your knitting pattern.
  2. Knit and shape the first side of the neckline.
  3. Rehang the scrapped-off stitches.
  4. Restart the stitch pattern.
  5. Knit and shape the second side of the neckline.

Watch the video below for a demonstration.

Step-by-Step Checklist

  1. Record the stitch pattern row number. For example, write down Row 5.
  2. Record the needle positions for the stitches you’ll scrap off, such as L65 and R65. Mark those positions on the needle bed or take a clear close-up photo so you can check them later.
  3. Follow your knitting pattern to scrap off the stitches for one half of the neckline.

    Tip. To avoid interrupting the stitch pattern, knit a few rows by hand in waste yarn before scrapping off.

  4. Knit and shape the first side of the neckline.
  5. With the wrong side facing you and the carriage on the left, rehang the scrapped-off stitches on the same needles they came from.
  6. Use the arrow keys to set the display to the stitch pattern row number you recorded.
  7. With all needles in B position and both PART buttons engaged, make a free pass to the right.
  8. Use your needle bed marks or photo to confirm that the correct needles are selected.
  9. Release the PART buttons, then set the cam buttons for your stitch pattern.

    Tip. Use the MC button for Fair Isle, the TUCK buttons for tuck, or the PART buttons for slip.

  10. With the carriage on the right, thread the carriage.
  11. Knit and shape the second side of the neckline according to your knitting pattern.

About Tuck Stitch

Tuck stitch is a great way to add texture and interest to your knitting.

A needle that tucks holds its existing stitch and catches the working yarn without knitting it off. When that needle knits again, it works the held stitch and the tuck loops together.

Once you understand how your machine makes tuck stitches, try these variations.

  • Change how many rows a needle tucks.
  • Change which needles are selected.
  • Change how many rows you knit between tucks.
  • Put some needles out of work to change the texture.
  • Add color.
  • Combine tuck with other stitch patterns.
Check out the Knit it Now Stitch Library for Tuck and Tuck lace Inspiration! Here are a few samples:

Tuck Lace is simply tuck stitch with needles out of work. The needles out of work can create airy, open fabric that resembles lace ... without any stitch transfers!
One of the more difficult things for knitters is deciphering what needles to put out of work.
REMEMBER: By default, stitch patterns are centered on the needlebed.
Examine this example:
  • The stitch pattern repeat is 8 stitches. Centered on the machine would put needles left 1-4 and needles right 1-4 in work
  • The O symbol at the bottom of the pattern indicates the needles out of work.
  • Any white squares will tuck
  • The best way to test your setup is to "Dry Knit"
  • Unless you manually change the position of the stitch pattern, it will be centered on the machine.

Knitting in fairisle or two colors across each row is a staple technique for machine knitters.
By Placing yarn in each yarn feeder of the carriage and setting the machine correctly, you can knit stranded knitting in a fraction of the time of knitting it by hand
Because you are knitting multiple colors across the row, the yarns are carried across the purl side of the knitting. These are called Floats .
When choosing a stitch pattern, keep in mind the length of the floats. It's recommended that the floats be no more than 5 stitches .. many knitters try to keep floats to 3 stitches.
The memo numbers of your stitch pattern alert you when to change colors.
Take time to master fairisle knitting with so many stitch patterns available, adding fairisle will make your knitting special.
Tell a hand knitter that you can knit a fairisle hat in an afternoon and they will be amazed.
(PLUS your fairisle will look sooooo much better than hand knitting. )

Lace Carriage on Brother machines selects the needles depending on your patterning device (electronics) AND transfers the stitches to form eyelets.
When the transfers are complete you are instructed to knit with the "K" (main)carriage. The Lace carriage DOES NOT KNIT.
This machine can produce 2 types of lace:
  • Plain lace (eyelets)
  • Fine lace: Instead of transferring an entire stitch, forming an eyelet, Fine Lace transfers one leg of a stitch to the adjacent needle. In other words, the stitch is shared between 2 needles. This creates an interesting texture without holes.

As you scan through the stitch pattern charts in the back of the Stitch World Book, you'll notice the lace stitch patterns look very different than other stitch patterns. The black squares are spread apart.
The black squares represent selected needles
The Memo numbers indicate the number of rows to knit with the "K" Carriage
The Main "K" carriage:
  • Forms stitches and knits
  • DOES NOT read the stitch pattern
  • DOES NOT select needles
  • Advances the manual row counter

The "K" carriage is always set for plain knitting.
The Lace Carriage:
  • Reads the stitch pattern
  • Selects needles
  • Transfers stitches
  • DOES NOT advance the row counter
The lace carriage ALWAYS begins and ends on the left.
No matter how many transfer rows of the sequence of knitting, the lace carriage ALWAYS begins and ends on the left. This may mean passing the carriage without any needles being selected or transferred.

Picture this:
  • You have a knitting machine with 200 needles.
  • You use a carriage to quickly knit 200 needles with the pass of the carriage
  • Imagine cloning that needlebed, turning it 180° and positioning the needles facing each other.

Now you have a setup that can not only create purl stitches, but knit stitches as well. That is the basic idea of a knitting machine ribber.
Imagine being able to knit k1, p1 ribbing with the pass of the carriage ... but wait! There's so much more!
A bit of advice:
If you are just getting started with machine knitting and have a ribber, be kind to yourself and take this advice.
Put the ribber aside for a while ... master the single bed BEFORE adding the ribber to the equation.
Learn and understand the settings for your machine. Practice with a few different yarns, learn to read and follow patterns ... get some successes under your belt before adding the ribber.
Trust me .... been there ... done that

Racking refers to the position of the ribber needles in relation to the main bed needles.
"P" Pitch: Ribber and Main Bed Needles are directly across from each other.
"H" Half Pitch: Ribber and Main Bed Needles alternate
"Swinging" the ribber can be used in cast on methods as well as for creating beautiful and unusual knit and purl stitch patterns.

On the Brother 930/940, racking involves sliding the Half Pitch Lever:
"P" for pitch (ribber and main bed needles are directly across from each other)
"H" for half pitch (ribber and main bed needles alternate)

Don't Skip This!
No matter how you set the tension dials, your ribber and main bed will knit at different tensions.
For success with any ribbing technique, take time to learn the differences for YOUR machine.

The full needle rib technique uses all needles on the ribber and main bed at the same time. It is used to create beautiful reversible fabrics and often used to create multi-color double bed jacquard
For success with this technique, it is CRITICAL that you understand the concept of Full vs Half pitch (the position of the needles of both beds)

Fun with Flat Ribs

Another variation of Full Needle Rib is Flat Rib. Instead of all needles being in work, selected needles on either the main bed or ribber are put into work, creating knit stitch texture against a purl background.

slides.caption: Half Milano, also called Long Stitch, is a variation of full needle rib. It’s the basis for several other ribber stitch patterns.
Put all needles on both beds in work. Cast on and establish full needle rib.
Set the ribber carriage to slip in one direction by raising one cam lever. On the first pass, the main bed knits and the ribber slips. On the return pass, both beds knit. Repeat these two passes.
Look at the side where the needles knit on every pass. It looks like stockinette.
Turn the swatch over. The stitches that slipped on alternate passes look longer.
You can set either bed to slip. Choose which side of the fabric you want to show on the outside of your project.

This technique produces a wide, thick, stretchy fabric that has many uses.

Set up for English Rib:
Similar to English Rib, Fisherman Rib is a wide, thick, stretchy fabric knit in a 1x1 needle arrangement with tuck stitch on BOTH needlebeds.

Settings:
Ribber:
  • Tucking Lever: T
  • LEFT Cam Lever up P-R
Main Bed:
  • Change Knob: N
  • Right Tuck Cam button engaged (in)

With the setting shown above, the beds alternate tucking. As one bed tucks, the other knits:

Ribber Main Bed
Carriage on the right, knit left Tuck Knit
Carriage on the left, knit right: Knit Tuck
Carriage on the right, knit left Tuck Knit
Carriage on the left, knit right: Knit Tuck

If you have a ribber, you can set your machine to knit in the round and eliminate seaming tubular pieces. Yes, there are some limitations, but this technique is very useful for a number of applications.
  • What about quickly knitting hats and caps without a seam?
  • Knit socks in the round
  • You can even knit the body of a plain garment to the armholes, then split the fronts and backs and knit them on the single bed.
    • This tutorial assumes you are familiar with setting up and knitting Full Needle Rib .
    REMEMBER: 2 passes of the carriage (left then right) equal one row of knitting

Your manual (pages 30-31) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for Circular.
Use the checklist below:
  • Needle Arrangement: All needles in Work (Pitch "H")
  • Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord
  • Hang Ribber Cast on Comb
  • Knit a few rows plain
  • Change to Circular knitting arrangement (slip settings)
    • Main bed part button (LEFT part button engaged)
    • RIGHT ribber cam button up (P-R)
  • Knit to the right and left - each pass on only 1 bed.
  • Knit a few rows in waste yarn
  • Knit 1 row with ravel cord (1 pass on each bed)
  • Change to main yarn and continue knitting in the round

This variation of Circular (tubular) knitting leaves one edge open and creates a very wide fabric. Imagine knitting a piece that is double the width of your needlebed!
Master the use of the slip setting on your carriages and give half circular knitting a try..
REMEMBER: 2 passes of the carriage (left then right) or (right then left) equal one row of knitting.

Your manual (pages 31-32) contains excellent step-by-step instructions for U-Knitting.
Use the checklist below:
  • Needle Arrangement: All needles in Work (Pitch "H")
  • Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord
  • Hang Ribber Cast on Comb
  • Knit a few rows plain
  • Change to U-Knitting knitting arrangement (slip settings)
    2 Steps
    Step 1:
    • Main bed part button (LEFT part button engaged)
    • RIGHT ribber cam button up (P-R)

    Step 2: (reverse the slip settings)
    • Main bed part button (RIGHTpart button engaged)
    • LEFT ribber cam button up (P-R)
  • Knit step 1 - each pass on only 1 bed.
  • Change settings: Knit Step 2
  • Knit a few rows in waste yarn
  • Knit 1 row with ravel cord (1 pass on each bed)
  • Change to main yarn and continue knitting, ,alternating Step 1 and Step 2 for U Knitting

components.html: Change colors

The KRC button will "separate" a stitch pattern for use with double bed jacquard. Double Bed Jacquard is multi-color slip with colors changing every 2 rows. In the following example, the 6 row (even number of rows) fairisle design is "separated" to a 6 color design. Notice the color memo numbers on the separated stitch pattern.
If you are new to Double Bed Jacquard, it is highly recommended you use the built-in stitch patterns in the Stitch World book that are already separated. ( Patterns 368-394. or the patterns in the Ribber manual) Once you get more familiar with this technique you can experiment with your own separations.
If you are using a stitch pattern that is already "separated" (ie from DesignaKnit) you don't need to use the KRC button.

Bird's Eye Backing


Instead of stripes on the back of the DBJ, use the lili (lily) buttons to "distort" the stripes and create a bird's eye backing.
  • This technique slips every other needle alternating every row.
  • Notice that not only the backing is distorted but the front side of the knitting is also impacted
  • Also be aware that using the bird's eye technique impacts gauge. Be sure to swatch using the technique.
  • Shown here is Bird's Eye with stripes, but the technique also can be used while patterning on the main bed
The setup for bird's eye backing:
  • EVEN number of needles on the ribber. As shown in the diagram, the 2nd needle from the end is selected IN THE DIRECTION OF THE CARRIAGE. It it critical that an even number of stitches are in work.
  • LILI buttons (KR change Knob to ) (push the buttons IN to turn)
  • Tucking lever to "R"
  • Holding Cam levers to "N" (normal)
  • Cam levers (L and R) to P-R
  • Slide lever to lili (controls the size of the ribber stitches)

The best way to understand this technique is to try it.
Be sure you have all the "pieces" in place and you are familiar with each of them:

Practice Double-Bed Jacquard

  1. Cast on using the main bed only. Knit a one-color slip stitch pattern using one of patterns 323–367.
  2. Still using the main bed only, practice two-color slip stitch using one of patterns 368–394.
  3. Engage the ribber and set up for full needle rib.
  4. Attach the ribber color changer and knit two-row stripes in full needle rib.
  5. Choose a ribber jacquard pattern from patterns 512–531 and knit it with two colors per row.
  6. Knit a ribber jacquard pattern with three or four colors per row.
